Brachioradialis bends the elbow and is active whether the palm faces up, sideways or down. Anatomy references describe it as strongest with the forearm half-turned (thumb up). From a fully palm-up or palm-down start it also turns the forearm back toward thumb-up. It does not cross the wrist.

Each catalog exercise the forearm atlas maps has one default variant (cat-<id>) with its execution spelled out: organization, forearm orientation, wrist position, grip, straps, laterality, measure, deliberate hold, and an elbow angle only where the exercise defines one. Each mapping names one muscle, one joint action, a relationship (direct, contributing, stabilizer, incidental) and a muscle mode (dynamic or isometric) separately, so one set can be dynamic elbow flexion and isometric wrist stabilization at once. Mappings are by catalog id; no name matching. A mapping is reviewed when the muscle's action is sourced (anatomy tables S4, S7, S8, the arm reference M8) and the relationship is explained in its rationale; EMG sources (S2, S3, M1, M2, M5-M7) are cited only for what they measured. Everything else stays draft and is shown as pending review, never counted. FDS and FDP are always credited together as shared: nothing in an ordinary grip separates them. Grip during rows, pulldowns, pull-ups, deadlifts, shrugs and hangs is incidental and is not earned by a set logged with straps. No percentage splits between muscles, no mapping credits every forearm muscle, the hand's own muscles are not credited to the forearm, and a broad 'forearms' tag on an unmapped exercise stays region-level.

The finger parts of FDS can be recruited selectively to some degree, with coupling between fingers. When one finger flexed at half its maximum force, fewer than half of the motor units serving the other fingers' parts became active, and units serving a neighbouring finger were recruited most readily. This supports describing finger actions; it does not show that one finger's part can be trained in isolation.

Whether forearm position changes how hard the brachioradialis works when bending the elbow is unsettled. A surface-EMG study of 16 people found its share differed with the palm down compared with palm up or thumb up; a fine-wire EMG study of 10 people found no difference between the three positions. Neither study measured growth.
Which kind of work a mapping counts as is set by the counting rule (specialization_exposure_v1), a Sports Genome choice; the sources speak to what the muscle does, not to how much it grows.
Winding by rolling the top of the roller away from you, palms down is a series of wrist flexions against the hanging weight, one of this muscle's main actions: direct, dynamic work.
Winding by rolling the top of the roller toward you, palms down is driven by the extensors; this muscle steadies and returns the hand between turns: contributing, not direct.

Winding the roller moves each wrist through flexion and extension against the hanging weight, but which way it is wound (and so which group lifts and which lowers) is not recorded. Both groups are credited as contributing and shared, rather than as direct work for either.

With the palms down the biceps is at a mechanical disadvantage and the brachioradialis's share of elbow flexion changes (M1 measured the difference in pronation), so the reverse curl is a direct brachioradialis exercise.

Work tagged with the region in the exercise catalog but with no reviewed atlas mapping counts only at region level, never as work for a specific muscle. Draft mappings are shown as pending review and not counted. Unknown is never shown as zero. The region total counts distinct bouts that touched any of its muscles on that arm. It is not the sum of the muscle rows.
